title: Leverage: why winning strategy comes from strengths, differentiation and durability, not fixing weaknesses
summary: Jason Cohen argues effective strategy rests on three nested layers of leverage: strengths, differentiated strengths, and durable differentiated strengths (moats). He says to sidestep weaknesses rather than fix them, and shows how interlocking choices (Southwest) and competitor lock-in create lasting advantage.

principles.text: Win by leveraging strengths, not by shoring up weaknesses.
principles.quote: Leveraging strengths is the only way to do great work. (Not "fixing weaknesses.")

principles.text: Fixing a weakness is hard and usually yields only neutral, so lean on innate greatness instead.
principles.quote: Reversing weakness is hard, painful, likely to result in something merely neutral, not great, and is at high risk of failing completely.

principles.text: Avoid weaknesses through target market, persona and product choices rather than fixing them.
principles.quote: Better is to avoid weaknesses through decisions on target market, target personas, and product

principles.text: Use the tool or language you already know, since it leverages your scarcest resource: time.
principles.quote: the best answer to "what tool/language/framework/process should I use to do ______?" is "the one you already know."

principles.text: For weaknesses that only matter past a threshold (like uptime), set an agreed threshold and invest only when it is breached.
principles.quote: while the metric exceeds the threshold, we do not attempt to improve it--that's like over-investing in a weakness that will never become a strength.

principles.text: Exploit competitors' ossified structure (cost base, values, platform trade-offs) to create differentiation they cannot match.
principles.quote: A competitor with a high cost structure *must* charge high prices, therefore a strategy of have "40% of the features at 10% of the price" leverages a point of differentiation that the competitor cannot match.
